Everyday Chemical Changes & Chemical Reactions (Page 1)

Consider the following common situations from daily life and observe what changes take place:

  • Milk left in summer: Milk left at room temperature during summers curdles and turns sour due to lactic acid fermentation.
  • Iron article in humidity: An iron tawa/pan/nail exposed to humid atmosphere develops a reddish-brown coating of rust.
  • Grapes fermenting: Sugars present in grapes get converted into alcohol and carbon dioxide by yeast enzymes.
  • Cooking food: Raw vegetables and grain undergo irreversible complex biochemical changes when food is cooked.
  • Digestion: Complex food nutrients are broken down into simple absorbable units like glucose inside our body.
  • Respiration: We inhale oxygen to oxidise glucose in our body cells, producing energy, carbon dioxide, and water.
📌 Core Takeaway: In all the above situations, the nature and identity of the initial substance have changed. Whenever a chemical change occurs, we can say that a chemical reaction has taken place.
🧪

Activity 1.1 — Burning of a Magnesium Ribbon (Pages 1–2)

⚠️ CAUTION: This activity requires the teacher's assistance. It is recommended that students wear suitable eye-protection goggles.
  1. Step 1: Clean a magnesium ribbon about 3–4 cm long by gently rubbing its surface with sandpaper.
  2. Step 2: Hold the magnesium ribbon firmly with a pair of metal tongs.
  3. Step 3: Burn it using a spirit lamp or Bunsen burner, keeping it as far away from your eyes as possible.
  4. Step 4: Collect the white ash so formed in a clean watch-glass placed underneath (as shown in Fig. 1.1).
✅ Observation & Inference
1. Dazzling White Flame: The magnesium ribbon burns with an intense, dazzling white flame.
2. Formation of White Powder: It changes into a white powder, which is magnesium oxide (MgO).
3. Chemical Reaction Occurred: Magnesium combines vigorously with atmospheric oxygen: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s).

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for dazzling white flame + 1 mark for identifying white powder as magnesium oxide).

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.1

Burning of a magnesium ribbon in air and collection of magnesium oxide in a watch-glass (Page 1).

  • Cleaning with Sandpaper: Magnesium metal is reactive and forms a protective, inert layer of basic magnesium oxide/carbonate upon standing in air. Rubbing with sandpaper removes this coating so the pure metal catches fire smoothly.
  • Pair of Tongs: Essential laboratory precaution to prevent thermal burns during the highly exothermic combustion.
  • Watch-Glass Collection: Collects the white powdery residue of magnesium oxide (MgO).

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.1 Burning of a magnesium ribbon in air and collection of magnesium oxide in a watch-glass

📌 Key Takeaway: Direct combination of a metal with oxygen releasing intense thermal and luminous energy.

🖼️ Fig. 1.1 – Burning of Magnesium Ribbon

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 1

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 1.1 • Burning of Magnesium Ribbon

Q1: Why should a magnesium ribbon be cleaned with sandpaper before burning in air?

✅ Answer Magnesium ribbon is cleaned before burning to remove the protective layer of magnesium oxide (and basic magnesium carbonate) that forms on its surface by slow reaction with atmospheric oxygen and moisture. Removing this unreactive coating allows the underlying pure magnesium to ignite easily.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for identifying the protective oxide layer + 1 mark for allowing pure metal to come in direct contact with air/oxygen).

Q2: What is the chemical nature of the white ash formed? How can it be confirmed experimentally?

✅ Answer The white ash is magnesium oxide (MgO), which is basic in nature. When dissolved in water, it forms magnesium hydroxide [MgO + H2O → Mg(OH)2], which turns red litmus paper blue, confirming its basic character.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for identifying basic metal oxide + 1 mark for red litmus turning blue via hydroxide solution).

🔬

Activities 1.2 & 1.3 — Testing for Chemical Reactions (Page 2)

🧪 Activity 1.2 — Precipitation of Lead Iodide
  • Take a clear lead nitrate [Pb(NO3)2] solution in a test tube.
  • Add colourless potassium iodide (KI) solution to it.
Observation: An instantaneous bright yellow precipitate of lead iodide (PbI2) appears:
Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI2(s)↓ + 2KNO3(aq).
🔥 Activity 1.3 — Reaction of Zinc with Acid
  • Take a few zinc granules in a conical flask or test tube.
  • Add dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl) or sulphuric acid (H2SO4). (CAUTION: Handle acid with care).
Observation: Gas bubbles evolve rapidly around the zinc granules. Touching the bottom of the flask reveals it has become warm (temperature increases).
Zn(s) + H2SO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g)↑ + Heat.

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.2

Formation of hydrogen gas by the action of dilute sulphuric acid on zinc (Page 2).

  • Zinc Granules: Active metal positioned above hydrogen in the reactivity series.
  • Evolution of Hydrogen Gas: Escapes through the glass delivery tube inserted through a tight cork.
  • Exothermic Temperature Rise: Reaction releases heat energy, warming the conical flask.

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.2 Formation of hydrogen gas by the action of dilute sulphuric acid on zinc

📌 Key Takeaway: Confirms a chemical reaction through simultaneous gas evolution and temperature increase.

🖼️ Fig. 1.2 – Reaction of Zinc with Acid

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 2

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 1.2 • Zinc & Dilute Acid

Q1: How is the gas evolved in Fig. 1.2 tested in the laboratory?

✅ Answer Bring a burning candle or splinter near the mouth of the delivery tube. The hydrogen gas burns with a characteristic 'pop' sound, confirming its presence.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for burning with a pop sound).

Q2: What changes occur in the flask during this reaction? Is the process endothermic or exothermic?

✅ Answer Zinc granules gradually dissolve, effervescence occurs as hydrogen gas bubbles form, and the flask becomes warm. Because heat is liberated, the reaction is exothermic.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for observation of bubbles/warm flask + 1 mark for stating exothermic nature).

Characteristics That Determine a Chemical Reaction (Page 2)

From Activities 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3, we conclude that any of the following 4 distinct observations confirms that a chemical reaction has taken place:

1 Change in State (e.g. solid wax burns to form liquid water & gaseous CO2)
2 Change in Colour (e.g. colourless solutions form yellow PbI2 precipitate)
3 Evolution of a Gas (e.g. zinc reacting with acid liberates H2 gas bubbles)
4 Change in Temperature (e.g. heat released in combustion or dissolution of quick lime)
📝

1.1 Chemical Equations (Pages 2–3)

Activity 1.1 can be described as: “When a magnesium ribbon is burnt in oxygen, it gets converted to magnesium oxide.” This sentence description is long. A more concise way is writing a word-equation:

Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide     (1.1)
(Reactants on LHS)                  (Product on RHS)

  • Reactants: The initial chemical substances that undergo chemical transformation in the reaction (written on the Left-Hand Side [LHS] with a plus sign + between them).
  • Products: The new chemical substances formed as a result of the reaction (written on the Right-Hand Side [RHS] with a plus sign + between them).
  • Reaction Arrow: The arrow → points towards the products and indicates the direction in which the chemical change proceeds.
✏️

1.1.1 Writing a Chemical Equation & Skeletal Equations (Page 3)

Chemical equations become far more concise and useful when we substitute words with chemical formulae. Representing magnesium burning in oxygen with chemical symbols:

Mg + O2 → MgO     (1.2)

Let us count and compare the number of atoms of each element on both sides of equation (1.2):

  • Magnesium (Mg): 1 atom on LHS • 1 atom on RHS (Balanced).
  • Oxygen (O): 2 atoms on LHS • only 1 atom on RHS (Unbalanced).
⚠️ Skeletal Chemical Equation: Because the number of oxygen atoms is not equal on both sides, the mass is not conserved. An unbalanced chemical equation where the number of atoms of one or more elements differs on LHS and RHS is called a skeletal chemical equation. Equation (1.2) is a skeletal equation for magnesium combustion.
⚖️

1.1.2 Balanced Chemical Equations (Pages 3–4)

Recall the fundamental Law of Conservation of Mass (studied in Class IX):

“Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.”

– Antoine Lavoisier

Meaning in Chemistry: The total mass of elements present in the products must equal the total mass of elements present in the reactants. Consequently, the total number of atoms of each element remains identical before and after a chemical reaction. Hence, every skeletal equation must be balanced.

Example: Balanced Equation for Activity 1.3

Word-equation: Zinc + Sulphuric acid → Zinc sulphate + Hydrogen
Chemical equation: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2     (1.3)

Element Number of Atoms in Reactants (LHS) Number of Atoms in Products (RHS) Balanced Status
Zn (Zinc) 1 1 Balanced ✓
H (Hydrogen) 2 2 Balanced ✓
S (Sulphur) 1 1 Balanced ✓
O (Oxygen) 4 4 Balanced ✓
✅ Result: Since the number of atoms of every element is identical on both sides of the arrow, equation (1.3) is a fully balanced chemical equation.
🪜

Mastering Equation Balancing — The 7-Step Hit-and-Trial Method (Pages 4–5)

Let us balance the following skeletal equation step-by-step:

Fe + H2O → Fe3O4 + H2     (1.4)
1
Box Formulae
2
Count Atoms
3
Balance Max Atoms (O)
4
Balance H Atoms
5
Balance Fe Atoms
6
Count & Verify
7
State Symbols
Step I — Draw Boxes Around Each Formula:
Draw boxes around each chemical formula. Do not alter or change anything inside the boxes while balancing!
[Fe] + [H2O] → [Fe3O4] + [H2]     (1.5)
Step II — Inventory Atoms on LHS and RHS:
Element Number of Atoms in Reactants (LHS) Number of Atoms in Products (RHS)
Fe (Iron)13
H (Hydrogen)22
O (Oxygen)14
Step III — Balance Compound with Maximum Atoms (Fe3O4 → Oxygen):
Select the compound with the maximum number of atoms, which is Fe3O4, and the element with the maximum atoms in it: Oxygen (4 on RHS, 1 on LHS).
Atoms of Oxygen In Reactants (LHS) In Products (RHS)
(i) Initial1 (in H2O)4 (in Fe3O4)
(ii) To balance1 × 44

Rule: We cannot change chemical subscripts! We place coefficient 4 in front of H2O as 4H2O (NEVER H2O4 or (H2O)4).
Partly balanced equation: Fe + 4H2O → Fe3O4 + H2     (1.6)

Step IV — Balance Hydrogen (H) Atoms:
LHS now has 4 × 2 = 8 hydrogen atoms, whereas RHS has only 2. To equalise, put coefficient 4 before H2 on RHS:
Atoms of Hydrogen In Reactants (LHS) In Products (RHS)
(i) Initial8 (in 4H2O)2 (in H2)
(ii) To balance82 × 4
Partly balanced equation: Fe + 4H2O → Fe3O4 + 4H2     (1.7)
Step V — Balance the Remaining Element (Iron, Fe):
RHS contains 3 atoms of iron (in Fe3O4), while LHS has 1 atom. Multiply Fe on LHS by 3:
Atoms of Iron (Fe) In Reactants (LHS) In Products (RHS)
(i) Initial1 (in Fe)3 (in Fe3O4)
(ii) To balance1 × 33
Equation becomes: 3Fe + 4H2O → Fe3O4 + 4H2     (1.8)
Step VI — Count and Verify Atoms on Both Sides:
Count atoms of each element on both sides:
3Fe + 4H2O → Fe3O4 + 4H2     (1.9)
  • Fe: 3 on LHS = 3 on RHS ✓
  • H: 8 on LHS = 8 on RHS ✓
  • O: 4 on LHS = 4 on RHS ✓
This method is known as the Hit-and-Trial Method because we make successive trials to balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients.
Step VII — Writing Symbols of Physical States:
Equation (1.9) does not specify the physical state of any reactant or product. To make chemical equations more informative, notations are added:
  • Solid state: (s)
  • Liquid state: (l)
  • Gaseous state: (g)
  • Aqueous solution (dissolved in water): (aq)
The complete balanced equation is:
3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) → Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g)     (1.10)

Note: The notation (g) with H2O indicates that water is supplied in the form of steam.

Specifying Reaction Conditions (Temperature, Pressure, Catalyst)

Specific external reaction conditions are placed above and/or below the arrow:

1. Methanol Synthesis:

CO(g) + 2H2(g) 340 atm
→ CH3OH(l)     (1.11)

2. Photosynthesis Reaction:

6CO2(aq) + 12H2O(l) Sunlight
→
Chlorophyll C6H12O6(aq) + 6O2(aq) + 6H2O(l)     (1.12)

🔍 Student Challenge from Textbook: Using the 7 steps above, can you balance equation (1.2) for the burning of magnesium ribbon?

✅ Balanced Solution

Skeletal: Mg + O2 → MgO

  1. Oxygen atoms: 2 on LHS, 1 on RHS → Multiply MgO by 2: Mg + O2 → 2MgO
  2. Magnesium atoms: 1 on LHS, 2 on RHS → Multiply Mg on LHS by 2: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO
  3. Add physical states: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s) ✓

NCERT In-Text Questions (Page 6)

Q1. Why should a magnesium ribbon be cleaned before burning in air?
✅ Model Answer
1. Removal of Protective Oxide Layer (Marking Keyword): Magnesium is a reactive metal. When exposed to air, it reacts slowly with atmospheric oxygen to form a thin, inert protective coating of magnesium oxide [and basic magnesium carbonate, MgCO3·Mg(OH)2].
2. Direct Combustion in Air: This outer protective film hinders combustion. Cleaning the ribbon with sandpaper removes this oxide layer, allowing the fresh magnesium metal beneath to come into direct contact with atmospheric oxygen and burn smoothly.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for identifying the protective oxide/carbonate layer + 1 mark for allowing pure metal direct contact with oxygen for ignition).

Q2. Write the balanced equation for the following chemical reactions.
  1. (i) Hydrogen + Chlorine → Hydrogen chloride
  2. (ii) Barium chloride + Aluminium sulphate → Barium sulphate + Aluminium chloride
  3. (iii) Sodium + Water → Sodium hydroxide + Hydrogen
✅ Model Answer
(i) Hydrogen + Chlorine:
H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g)
(ii) Barium chloride + Aluminium sulphate:
3BaCl2(aq) + Al2(SO4)3(aq) → 3BaSO4(s)↓ + 2AlCl3(aq)
(iii) Sodium + Water:
2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g)↑ + Heat

📌 Marking Scheme: 3 marks — (1 mark for each correctly balanced chemical equation with correct stoichiometric coefficients).

Q3. Write a balanced chemical equation with state symbols for the following reactions.
  1. (i) Solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulphate in water react to give insoluble barium sulphate and the solution of sodium chloride.
  2. (ii) Sodium hydroxide solution (in water) reacts with hydrochloric acid solution (in water) to produce sodium chloride solution and water.
✅ Model Answer
(i) Barium chloride + Sodium sulphate:
BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) → BaSO4(s)↓ + 2NaCl(aq)
(White precipitate of barium sulphate forms in aqueous sodium chloride solution)
(ii) Sodium hydroxide + Hydrochloric acid:
NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)
(Neutralisation reaction between strong base and strong acid)

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for each balanced equation including complete state symbols: aq, s, l).

Quick Check: Objective Questions (Section 1.1)

1. MCQ: Which of the following is an essential requirement for a balanced chemical equation?

  1. Total number of molecules on LHS must equal total molecules on RHS
  2. Total number of atoms of each element on LHS must equal total atoms on RHS
  3. Physical states must be identical on both sides
  4. Coefficients must all be even integers
✅ Answer (B) Total number of atoms of each element on LHS must equal total atoms on RHS, strictly satisfying the Law of Conservation of Mass.

2. Fill-in-the-Blank: An unbalanced chemical equation where atom counts are unequal on LHS and RHS is termed a _________ chemical equation.

✅ Answer skeletal (or unbalanced) chemical equation.

3. True / False: In the equation 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) → Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g), the symbol (g) indicates that water reacts in the form of liquid steam droplets.

✅ Answer False. The symbol (g) indicates gaseous water, i.e., water in the form of steam, not liquid droplets.
🔑 Key Words — Section 1.1: Chemical Equations & Balancing ▼
Chemical Reaction Reactants Products Word-Equation Skeletal Equation Balanced Chemical Equation Hit-and-Trial Method Law of Conservation of Mass
  • Chemical Reaction: A process in which original substances break/form chemical bonds to produce new substances with entirely different chemical properties.
  • Reactants: The initial chemical substances that enter into and undergo chemical change during a reaction (written on LHS).
  • Products: The new chemical substances formed as a result of a chemical reaction (written on RHS).
  • Word-Equation: A concise chemical representation that links reactants and products using their standard chemical names and directional arrow.
  • Skeletal Chemical Equation: An unbalanced equation where the number of atoms of elements on LHS differs from RHS, violating mass conservation.
  • Balanced Chemical Equation: An equation having identical numbers of atoms of each element on both sides of the reaction arrow.
  • Hit-and-Trial Method: Systematic balancing technique using smallest whole-number stoichiometric coefficients without altering chemical formulas.
  • Law of Conservation of Mass: Matter can neither be created nor destroyed during a chemical reaction; total reactant mass equals total product mass.
🌱 2. Types of Chemical Reactions: Combination & Exothermic (Pages 6–8)
🔗

1.2 Types of Chemical Reactions — Bond Breaking & Making (Page 6)

In Class IX, we established that during a chemical reaction:

  • Atoms of one chemical element never transmute or change into atoms of another element.
  • Atoms do not disappear from the reaction mixture, nor do they appear from nowhere.
  • Fundamental Mechanism: Chemical reactions fundamentally involve the breaking of existing chemical bonds between reactant atoms and the making of new chemical bonds to produce novel product substances.
⚡

Activity 1.4 — Slaking of Lime: Combination Reaction (Page 6)

  1. Step 1: Take a small quantity (about 5 g) of calcium oxide (commonly called quick lime, CaO) in a dry glass beaker.
  2. Step 2: Slowly and carefully add water to the beaker.
  3. Step 3: Observe the vigorous hissing sound and touch the outside of the beaker gently (as shown in Fig. 1.3).
✅ Observation & Inference
1. Vigorous Reaction: Calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water with a hissing sound, forming a suspension.
2. Large Heat Evolution: A massive amount of heat is liberated; the beaker becomes extremely hot to the touch.
3. Formation of Slaked Lime: Quick lime and water unite to produce a single product, slaked lime [calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2].
CaO(s) + H2O(l) → Ca(OH)2(aq) + Heat     (1.13)
(Quick lime)                      (Slaked lime)

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for identifying vigorous reaction with temperature rise + 1 mark for balanced chemical equation).

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.3

Formation of slaked lime by the reaction of calcium oxide with water (Page 6).

  • Two Reactants to One Product: Two separate chemical substances—calcium oxide solid and liquid water—combine chemically to form only one single compound: aqueous calcium hydroxide.
  • Hissing Effervescence: Caused by localized boiling of water due to the intense exothermic energy release.
  • Clear Lime Water: Allowing the milky slaked lime suspension to settle gives clear lime water, used to test for carbon dioxide gas.

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.3 Formation of slaked lime by the reaction of calcium oxide with water

📌 Key Takeaway: Prime textbook prototype of both a Combination Reaction and an Exothermic Reaction.

🖼️ Fig. 1.3 – Formation of Slaked Lime

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 6

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 1.3 • Formation of Slaked Lime

Q1: Why does the beaker become hot to touch when water is added to quick lime in Fig. 1.3?

✅ Answer The reaction between quick lime (calcium oxide) and water is highly exothermic. It releases a substantial quantity of heat energy, which transfers to the beaker walls, causing a sharp temperature rise.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for identifying that the reaction is highly exothermic and releases heat).

Q2: Write the chemical name, common name, and chemical formula of the product formed in Fig. 1.3.

✅ Answer
  • Chemical Name: Calcium hydroxide
  • Common Name: Slaked lime (or lime water when dissolved in clear solution)
  • Chemical Formula: Ca(OH)2

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for chemical & common names + 1 mark for correct formula Ca(OH)2).

Definition & Core Examples of Combination Reactions (Pages 6–7)

Definition: A reaction in which a single product is formed from two or more reactants (elements or compounds) is known as a combination reaction.

More Examples of Combination Reactions:

🔥 (i) Burning of Coal

Carbon combines with atmospheric oxygen to form carbon dioxide gas:

C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g)     (1.15)

Two elements combine to form one compound.

💧 (ii) Formation of Water

Hydrogen gas combines with oxygen gas to yield liquid water:

2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(l)     (1.16)

Two gaseous elements combine into a single liquid compound.

🏛️

Do You Know? — The Chemistry of Whitewashing & Marble (Page 7)

A solution of slaked lime [Ca(OH)2] produced by reaction (1.13) is applied to coat walls during whitewashing.

  • Slow Reaction with Air: Calcium hydroxide reacts slowly with carbon dioxide (CO2) present in the air to form an insoluble, thin layer of calcium carbonate (CaCO3) on the walls.
  • Shiny Finish after 2–3 Days: This protective calcium carbonate layer crystallizes after two to three days of whitewashing, imparting a lustrous, brilliant white shiny finish to the walls.
  • Fascinating Fact: The chemical formula for limestone, chalk, eggshells, and exquisite natural marble is identical: CaCO3!
Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) → CaCO3(s) + H2O(l)     (1.14)
(Calcium hydroxide)                  (Calcium carbonate / Marble)
♨️

Exothermic Chemical Reactions (Pages 7–8)

Definition: Reactions in which heat energy is released along with the formation of products are called exothermic chemical reactions.

Everyday & Industrial Examples of Exothermic Reactions:

  • (i) Combustion of Natural Gas (Methane): Methane gas burns cleanly in air, liberating carbon dioxide, steam, and thermal energy:
    CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g) + Heat Energy     (1.17)
  • (ii) Respiration — The Cellular Energy Engine: We require energy to stay alive, derived from the food we consume. During digestion, carbohydrate-rich foods (rice, potatoes, bread) are broken down into simple glucose (C6H12O6). In our body cells, glucose reacts with inhaled oxygen to release continuous life-sustaining energy:
    C6H12O6(aq) + 6O2(aq) → 6CO2(aq) + 6H2O(l) + Energy     (1.18)
    Because energy is liberated, respiration is unequivocally an exothermic process!
  • (iii) Decomposition of Organic Vegetable Matter: The microbial decomposition of vegetable waste into organic compost in compost pits releases noticeable warmth and is an exothermic process.
🔍 Textbook Inquiry Solved (Page 7): “Identify the type of reaction taking place in Activity 1.1, where heat is given out along with the formation of a single product.”
Answer: The burning of magnesium ribbon in air (2Mg + O2 → 2MgO + Heat) is both a Combination Reaction (two elements form one product) and an Exothermic Reaction (liberates heat and light).
⚡

Quick Check: Objective Questions (Section 1.2.1)

1. MCQ: When slaked lime is applied to walls during whitewashing, the shiny white coating formed after 2–3 days is chemically:

  1. Calcium oxide [CaO]
  2. Calcium carbonate [CaCO3]
  3. Calcium bicarbonate [Ca(HCO3)2]
  4. Calcium sulphate [CaSO4]
✅ Answer (B) Calcium carbonate (CaCO3), formed by slow reaction with atmospheric CO2.

2. Assertion & Reason:
Assertion (A): Respiration is considered an exothermic reaction.
Reason (R): During respiration, glucose combines with oxygen in cells to release energy.

  1. Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
  2. Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
  3. A is true, but R is false
  4. A is false, but R is true
✅ Answer (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and R directly explains why respiration liberates energy and is classified as exothermic.
🔑 Key Words — Section 1.2.1: Combination & Exothermic Reactions ▼
Combination Reaction Exothermic Reaction Quick Lime Slaked Lime Respiration Calcium Carbonate
  • Combination Reaction: A chemical reaction in which two or more reactant substances combine to form a single chemical product.
  • Exothermic Reaction: A reaction that releases thermal energy into the surrounding environment, causing the temperature to rise.
  • Quick Lime: Solid calcium oxide (CaO), an industrial chemical manufactured by calcining limestone.
  • Slaked Lime: Calcium hydroxide [Ca(OH)2], formed by the highly exothermic hydration of quick lime.
  • Respiration: An exothermic biochemical combustion reaction in living cells where glucose is oxidised by oxygen to produce ATP energy, water, and CO2.
  • Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3): Insoluble white solid compound that constitutes marble, limestone, and the shiny finish on whitewashed walls.
⚡ 3. Decomposition Reactions: Thermal, Electrolytic & Photochemical (Pages 8–10)
💥

1.2.2 Decomposition Reactions — Concept & Classification (Page 8)

Definition: A chemical reaction in which a single reactant breaks down into two or more simpler products upon supply of energy is known as a decomposition reaction.

Decomposition reactions are essentially the exact opposite of combination reactions. Because bond breaking requires energy input, decomposition reactions require external energy supplied as heat, electricity, or light.

🧪

Activity 1.5 — Thermal Decomposition of Ferrous Sulphate (Page 8)

  1. Step 1: Take about 2 g of green ferrous sulphate crystals (FeSO4•7H2O) in a clean, dry boiling tube.
  2. Step 2: Note the pale-green colour of the hydrated crystals.
  3. Step 3: Heat the boiling tube over the flame of a burner or spirit lamp as shown in Fig. 1.4.
  4. Step 4: Observe the colour change and carefully waft the evolved gas gently towards your nose.
✅ Observation & Working
1. Dehydration (Loss of Water of Crystallisation): Green crystals (FeSO4•7H2O) initially lose 7 water molecules, turning into anhydrous white FeSO4.
2. Colour Change to Reddish-Brown: On further heating, white anhydrous FeSO4 decomposes into a reddish-brown solid residue of ferric oxide (Fe2O3).
3. Odour of Burning Sulphur: Two acidic, choking gases evolve: colourless sulphur dioxide (SO2) and sulphur trioxide (SO3).
2FeSO4(s) Heat
→ Fe2O3(s) + SO2(g) + SO3(g)     (1.19)
(Green ferrous sulphate)      (Reddish-brown ferric oxide)    (Pungent choking gases)

📌 Marking Scheme: 3 marks — (1 mark for colour change pale green → reddish brown + 1 mark for characteristic smell of burning sulphur + 1 mark for balanced equation).

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.4

Correct way of heating the boiling tube containing crystals of ferrous sulphate and of smelling the odour (Page 8).

  • Dry Boiling Tube: Standard test tubes crack under strong heating; hard borosilicate boiling tubes prevent thermal shattering.
  • Laboratory Safety Rule: Never point the open mouth of the boiling tube at yourself or your laboratory neighbours, as hot corrosive fumes can violently spurt out.
  • Wafting Technique: Gently fan the vapours towards your nose with your hand rather than inhaling directly over the tube mouth, protecting nasal membranes from toxic SO2.

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.4 Correct way of heating the boiling tube containing crystals of ferrous sulphate and of smelling the odour

📌 Key Takeaway: Laboratory safety protocol when generating hazardous choking sulphur gases during thermal decomposition.

🖼️ Fig. 1.4 – Heating Ferrous Sulphate

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 8

Q1: State two laboratory precautions illustrated in Fig. 1.4 during the heating of crystals.

✅ Answer
  1. Do not point the mouth of the boiling tube towards yourself or any neighbouring student.
  2. Waft the evolved gas gently towards your nose with your hand instead of smelling it directly.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for each valid safety precaution).

Q2: Name the two gaseous products formed in Fig. 1.4 and state their action on moist blue litmus paper.

✅ Answer The gaseous products are sulphur dioxide (SO2) and sulphur trioxide (SO3). Being non-metallic acidic oxides, both gases turn moist blue litmus paper red.

Industrial Thermal Decomposition: Limestone to Quick Lime (Page 8)

Decomposition of calcium carbonate to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide on heating is a cornerstone industrial reaction:

CaCO3(s) Heat
→ CaO(s) + CO2(g)     (1.20)
(Limestone)                      (Quick lime)              (Carbon dioxide)

Industrial Application: Calcium oxide (quick lime) has myriad industrial uses; its most prominent application is as a key raw material in the manufacture of cement and glass.

📌 Rule: When a decomposition reaction is carried out by heating, it is termed a thermal decomposition reaction.

Activity 1.6 — Thermal Decomposition of Lead Nitrate (Pages 8–9)

  1. Step 1: Take about 2 g of white lead nitrate powder [Pb(NO3)2] in a dry boiling tube.
  2. Step 2: Hold the boiling tube securely with a pair of metal tongs.
  3. Step 3: Heat it strongly over the flame of a burner (as shown in Fig. 1.5).
✅ Observation & Working
1. Emission of Dense Brown Fumes: Copious brown fumes are emitted. These distinctive fumes consist of nitrogen dioxide (NO2) gas.
2. Yellow Solid Residue: A solid residue of lead(II) oxide (PbO) remains in the tube, which is reddish-brown when hot and turns distinct yellow upon cooling.
3. Colourless Gas Evolved: Oxygen gas (O2) is also produced, which rekindles a glowing wooden splint.
2Pb(NO3)2(s) Heat
→ 2PbO(s) + 4NO2(g) + O2(g)     (1.21)
(White lead nitrate)        (Yellow lead oxide)    (Brown fumes)    (Colourless)

📌 Marking Scheme: 3 marks — (1 mark for identifying brown NO2 fumes + 1 mark for yellow PbO residue + 1 mark for balanced equation).

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.5

Heating of lead nitrate and emission of nitrogen dioxide (Page 8).

  • Pair of Tongs: Essential lab equipment holding the boiling tube at an incline during vigorous thermal cracking.
  • Brown Fumes of NO2: Characteristic diagnostic visual marker in CBSE board practical and theoretical exams.
  • Yellow Lead Monoxide (PbO): Adheres to the boiling tube walls, solidifying into a yellow glaze upon cooling.

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.5 Heating of lead nitrate and emission of nitrogen dioxide

📌 Key Takeaway: Thermal breakdown of a metal nitrate producing a metal oxide, toxic brown nitrogen dioxide, and oxygen gas.

🖼️ Fig. 1.5 – Heating of Lead Nitrate

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 8

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 1.5 • Lead Nitrate Decomposition

Q1: Name the gas responsible for the brown fumes observed in Fig. 1.5 and state its nature.

✅ Answer The brown fumes are nitrogen dioxide (NO2). It is an acidic gas that dissolves in water to form nitrous and nitric acids.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for correctly identifying nitrogen dioxide / NO2).

Q2: What remains in the boiling tube after complete thermal decomposition in Fig. 1.5?

✅ Answer A solid residue of lead(II) oxide (PbO) remains, which appears reddish-brown when hot and distinct yellow when cold.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for lead(II) oxide / PbO with yellow colour specification).

Activity 1.7 — Electrolysis of Water (Electrolytic Decomposition) (Page 9)

⚠️ CAUTION: Testing of evolved gases with a burning candle must be performed strictly by or under the direct supervision of the teacher.
  1. Step 1: Take a plastic mug. Drill two holes at its base and fit rubber stoppers tightly.
  2. Step 2: Insert two carbon (graphite) electrodes into these stoppers as shown in Fig. 1.6.
  3. Step 3: Connect the electrodes to the terminals of a 6-volt battery via connecting wires and a switch.
  4. Step 4: Fill the mug with water until the graphite electrodes are completely immersed. Add a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid to increase electrical conductivity.
  5. Step 5: Fill two identical graduated test tubes with water and carefully invert them over the two carbon electrodes.
  6. Step 6: Switch on the direct electric current and leave the apparatus undisturbed for 15–20 minutes.
✅ Observation & Working
1. Continuous Bubble Formation: Gas bubbles evolve at both electrodes, displacing water downward by downward displacement.
2. 2:1 Volume Ratio: The volume of gas collected in the test tube over the Cathode (Negative Terminal) is exactly twice the volume of gas collected over the Anode (Positive Terminal).
3. Confirmatory Candle Test:
  • Cathode Gas: Ignites with a distinct 'pop' sound → Hydrogen gas (H2).
  • Anode Gas: Makes a burning candle/splinter burn brightly or rekindles a glowing splint → Oxygen gas (O2).
2H2O(l) Electric Current
→ 2H2(g) [at cathode] + O2(g) [at anode]

📌 Marking Scheme: 3 marks — (1 mark for identifying H2 at cathode & O2 at anode + 1 mark for 2:1 volume ratio + 1 mark for confirmatory tests).

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.6

Electrolysis of water (Page 9).

  • Graphite Electrodes: Chemically inert carbon rods that conduct electric current without reacting with water or acid.
  • Role of Dilute H2SO4: Pure distilled water is a very poor conductor of electricity. Adding a few drops of acid provides free mobile ions (H+, SO42−), making water conducting.
  • Cathode vs Anode: Cathode attracts H+ ions (producing H2 gas); Anode attracts OH− ions (releasing O2 gas).
  • Stoichiometric Explanation: Because every water molecule consists of 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom (ratio 2 : 1), water electrolysis produces exactly twice the volume of hydrogen as oxygen.

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.6 Electrolysis of water

📌 Key Takeaway: Electric current decomposes water into hydrogen and oxygen in a precise 2:1 volumetric ratio.

🖼️ Fig. 1.6 – Electrolysis of Water

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 9

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 1.6 • Electrolysis of Water

Q1: Why is the volume of gas collected over one electrode double that over the other in Fig. 1.6?

✅ Answer Water (H2O) is composed of hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a 2 : 1 ratio by volume. When water decomposes electrolytically, two volumes of hydrogen gas are liberated at the cathode for every one volume of oxygen gas liberated at the anode:
2H2O(l) → 2H2(g) + O2(g).

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for chemical composition ratio 2 : 1 in H2O + 1 mark for balanced equation showing 2 volumes of H2 to 1 volume of O2).

Q2: Why are a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid added to the water in Fig. 1.6?

✅ Answer Pure distilled water is a covalent liquid and an extremely poor conductor of electricity (insulator). Adding a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid introduces free mobile ions (H+ and SO42−), which conduct electricity efficiently and enable electrolysis.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for stating that acid provides mobile ions to make water electrically conductive).

Activity 1.8 — Photochemical Decomposition of Silver Salts (Pages 9–10)

  1. Step 1: Place about 2 g of white silver chloride (AgCl) in a clean china dish.
  2. Step 2: Note its initial pure white colour.
  3. Step 3: Place the china dish near an open window under direct sunlight for a few hours (as shown in Fig. 1.7).
  4. Step 4: Observe the final colour of the substance.
✅ Observation & Working
1. White Turns Grey: The white silver chloride turns into a distinct greyish metallic powder upon exposure to sunlight.
2. Photolysis Reaction: Light photons break down silver chloride into metallic silver and greenish-yellow chlorine gas:
2AgCl(s) Sunlight
→ 2Ag(s) [Grey silver metal] + Cl2(g) [Chlorine gas]     (1.22)
3. Photolysis of Silver Bromide: Pale-yellow silver bromide (AgBr) decomposes similarly under sunlight:
2AgBr(s) Sunlight
→ 2Ag(s) + Br2(g)     (1.23)
4. Historic Application: These photochemical reactions of silver halides are extensively employed in black and white photography.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for colour change white → grey + 1 mark for balanced equation / application in black & white photography).

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.7

Silver chloride turns grey in sunlight to form silver metal (Page 9).

  • Sunlight as Energy Source: Photons of visible and UV light supply the exact activation energy required to split the Ag–Cl bond.
  • Metallic Silver Residue: Finely divided metallic silver particles scatter light, appearing dull grey.
  • Storage in Dark Bottles: In chemistry laboratories, solutions of AgCl and AgNO3 are stored in dark amber-coloured reagent bottles to block sunlight and prevent premature photolytic decomposition.

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.7 Silver chloride turns grey in sunlight to form silver metal

📌 Key Takeaway: Light-driven decomposition (photolysis) used historically in photographic emulsions.

🖼️ Fig. 1.7 – Photolysis of Silver Chloride

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 9

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 1.7 • Silver Chloride in Sunlight

Q1: Why does white silver chloride turn grey when exposed to sunlight in Fig. 1.7?

✅ Answer In the presence of sunlight, silver chloride undergoes photochemical decomposition into grey metallic silver and chlorine gas: 2AgCl(s) → 2Ag(s) + Cl2(g). The formation of finely divided silver metal causes the grey appearance.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for photochemical decomposition explanation + 1 mark for formation of metallic silver).

Q2: Name another compound that shows similar behaviour and state an important practical application.

✅ Answer Silver bromide (AgBr). Both reactions were historically used in black and white photography.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (0.5 mark for silver bromide + 0.5 mark for black and white photography).

Endothermic Reactions & Barium Hydroxide Activity (Page 10)

Definition: Chemical reactions in which energy is absorbed from the surroundings (in the form of heat, light, or electricity) are known as endothermic reactions.

Textbook Activity: Reaction of Barium Hydroxide with Ammonium Chloride (Page 10)

“Take about 2 g barium hydroxide in a test tube. Add 1 g of ammonium chloride and mix with the help of a glass rod. Touch the bottom of the test tube with your palm. What do you feel? Is this an exothermic or endothermic reaction?”

✅ Observation & Conclusion
1. Freezing Cold Sensation: The bottom of the test tube feels intensely cold; water droplets condense on the outer glass surface and can even freeze if placed on a moist wooden block.
2. Endothermic Reaction: The reaction absorbs massive thermal energy from the immediate surroundings, causing the temperature to plummet sharply:
Ba(OH)2•8H2O(s) + 2NH4Cl(s) → BaCl2(aq) + 2NH3(aq) + 10H2O(l) − Heat.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for observing sharp temperature decrease / bottom feels cold + 1 mark for classifying as endothermic reaction).

Q1. A solution of a substance ‘X’ is used for whitewashing.
  1. (i) Name the substance ‘X’ and write its formula.
  2. (ii) Write the reaction of the substance ‘X’ named in (i) above with water.

(i) Identity of Substance 'X' (Marking Keyword):
Substance 'X' is calcium oxide (commonly called quick lime).
Chemical formula: CaO.
(ii) Reaction with Water:
Calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water to form calcium hydroxide (slaked lime), releasing tremendous heat:
CaO(s) + H2O(l) → Ca(OH)2(aq) + Heat

Q2. Why is the amount of gas collected in one of the test tubes in Activity 1.7 double of the amount collected in the other? Name this gas.
✅ Model Answer
1. Molecular Formula of Water: Water consists of hydrogen and oxygen combined in the ratio of 2 : 1 by volume (H2O).
2. Electrolytic Stoichiometry: During electrolysis, 2 molecules of water decompose to yield 2 molecules of hydrogen gas and 1 molecule of oxygen gas:
2H2O(l) → 2H2(g) + O2(g)
3. Name of Gas (Marking Keyword): The gas with double volume collected at the cathode is Hydrogen (H2).

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for explaining 2:1 ratio from stoichiometry 2H2O → 2H2 + O2 + 1 mark for correctly identifying hydrogen gas).

  2. Nitrogen dioxide [NO2]

  4. Nitrogen pentoxide [N2O5]

🔑 Key Words — Section 1.2.2: Decomposition Reactions ▼
Decomposition Reaction Thermal Decomposition Electrolytic Decomposition Photochemical Decomposition Endothermic Reaction Ferric Oxide Nitrogen Dioxide
  • Decomposition Reaction: A reaction in which a single chemical substance breaks down into two or more simpler elements or compounds.
  • Thermal Decomposition: A decomposition process driven by thermal energy (heating).
  • Electrolytic Decomposition (Electrolysis): The cleavage of chemical bonds in an electrolyte by passing direct electrical current.
  • Photochemical Decomposition (Photolysis): Bond cleavage triggered by absorption of light energy (photons).
  • Endothermic Reaction: A chemical reaction that absorbs energy from its surroundings in the form of heat, light, or electricity.
  • Ferric Oxide (Fe2O3): Insoluble reddish-brown solid residue produced upon strong heating of ferrous sulphate.
  • Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2): Toxic, acidic gas visible as pungent brown fumes during nitrate decomposition.

Activity 1.9 — Iron Nails in Copper Sulphate Solution (Pages 10–11)

  1. Step 1: Take three clean iron nails and polish their surfaces by rubbing with sandpaper.
  2. Step 2: Set up two clean test tubes marked (A) and (B). In each test tube, take about 10 mL of deep-blue copper sulphate (CuSO4) solution.
  3. Step 3: Tie two iron nails securely with a thread and immerse them carefully into test tube (B) for about 20 minutes [Fig. 1.8 (a)]. Keep the third iron nail aside in dry air for comparison.
  4. Step 4: After 20 minutes, take out the iron nails from test tube (B).
  5. Step 5: Compare the blue colour intensity of solutions in test tubes (A) and (B), and compare the immersed iron nails with the control nail [Fig. 1.8 (b)].
✅ Observation & Working
1. Brownish Coating on Iron Nails: The submerged iron nails become coated with a thick, rough reddish-brown layer of copper metal [Cu].
2. Blue Solution Fades to Light Green: The intense sky-blue colour of copper sulphate solution gradually fades and turns into a pale light green solution of ferrous sulphate (FeSO4).
3. Chemical Reaction: Iron, being more electropositive and reactive than copper, displaces copper ions from solution:
Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) → FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)     (1.24)

📌 Marking Scheme: 3 marks — (1 mark for brown coating of copper + 1 mark for blue fading to light green ferrous sulphate + 1 mark for balanced equation).

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.8 (a)

Iron nails dipped in copper sulphate solution (Page 10).

  • Experimental Setup: Retort stand supporting a test tube containing 10 mL of aqueous blue CuSO4 solution.
  • Suspension with Thread: Two cleaned iron nails suspended without touching the tube base to ensure uniform chemical contact.
  • Duration of Contact: 20 minutes allow sufficient Fe2+ dissolution and Cu metal deposition.

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.8 (a) Iron nails dipped in copper sulphate solution

📌 Key Takeaway: Laboratory setup illustrating single displacement of a less reactive metal by a more reactive metal.

🖼️ Fig. 1.8 (a) – Nails Dipped in CuSO4

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 10

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 1.8 (a) • Nails in Copper Sulphate

Q1: Why are the iron nails cleaned with sandpaper before immersion in Fig. 1.8 (a)?

✅ Answer Iron nails are rubbed with sandpaper to remove rust (hydrated ferric oxide), dirt, and grease films from their surface, exposing pure metallic iron for unhindered displacement reaction with copper ions.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for removing rust/grease coating to expose pure active iron surface).

Q2: What will happen if a copper strip is dipped in ferrous sulphate solution instead? Explain.

✅ Answer No reaction occurs. Copper is significantly less reactive than iron in the reactivity series and cannot displace iron from ferrous sulphate solution: Cu(s) + FeSO4(aq) → No Reaction.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for 'no reaction' + 1 mark for stating that copper is less reactive than iron).

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.8 (b)

Iron nails and copper sulphate solutions compared before and after the experiment (Page 11).

  • Visual Comparison of Nails: Clean control nail (silvery-grey) vs experimental nail removed from test tube B (encrusted with reddish-brown copper deposit).
  • Visual Comparison of Solutions: Test tube A (retains original deep sky-blue colour of Cu2+ ions) vs Test tube B (discharged to pale green due to formation of Fe2+ ions).
  • Scientific Proof: Proves conclusively that iron atoms entered solution as Fe2+ ions while Cu2+ ions deposited onto the iron nail as metallic copper atoms.

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.8 (b) Iron nails and copper sulphate solutions compared before and after the experiment

📌 Key Takeaway: Direct visual verification of metal displacement via comparative control analysis.

🖼️ Fig. 1.8 (b) – Before & After Comparison

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 11

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 1.8 (b) • Before & After Comparison

Q1: Which chemical species is responsible for the pale green colour of the solution in test tube (B) in Fig. 1.8 (b)?

✅ Answer Ferrous ions (Fe2+) present in aqueous ferrous sulphate (FeSO4) solution.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for ferrous ions / Fe2+ / ferrous sulphate).

Q2: Account for the change in mass of the iron nail taken out of test tube (B).

✅ Answer The mass of the nail increases slightly because copper (atomic mass ≈ 63.5 u) deposited on the nail is heavier per atom than the iron (atomic mass ≈ 56 u) dissolved into solution.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for explaining mass increase due to higher atomic mass of deposited copper vs dissolved iron).

Displacement Reaction Definition & Reactivity Series Basis (Pages 11–12)

Definition: A chemical reaction in which a more reactive element displaces or removes another less reactive element from an aqueous solution of its compound is known as a displacement reaction.

Other Key Textbook Examples of Displacement Reactions:

⚪ Zinc Displacing Copper

Zinc is more reactive than copper:

Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)     (1.25)
(Silvery zinc)    (Blue)            (Colourless)      (Brown Cu)
🔘 Lead Displacing Copper

Lead is more reactive than copper:

Pb(s) + CuCl2(aq) → PbCl2(aq) + Cu(s)     (1.26)
(Lead metal)    (Greenish-blue)   (Colourless)      (Reddish-brown)
📌 Reactivity Hierarchy: Zinc (Zn) > Iron (Fe) > Lead (Pb) > Copper (Cu). Zinc and lead are both more reactive than copper, displacing it smoothly from its aqueous sulphate and chloride compounds.
🔄

Activity 1.10 — Precipitation of Barium Sulphate (Double Displacement) (Page 11)

  1. Step 1: Take about 3 mL of transparent sodium sulphate (Na2SO4) solution in a test tube.
  2. Step 2: In another test tube, take about 3 mL of colourless barium chloride (BaCl2) solution.
  3. Step 3: Mix the two solutions together as illustrated in Fig. 1.9.
  4. Step 4: Observe the instantaneous transformation.
✅ Observation & Working
1. White Insoluble Precipitate: An instantaneous opaque white precipitate separates out, rendering the liquid cloudy.
2. Formation of Barium Sulphate: The insoluble white substance is barium sulphate (BaSO4). The other product, sodium chloride (NaCl), remains dissolved in aqueous solution.
3. Exchange of Ions: Mutual ion exchange between barium cations (Ba2+) and sulphate anions (SO42−):
Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) → BaSO4(s)↓ + 2NaCl(aq)     (1.27)

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for observing white precipitate of BaSO4 + 1 mark for balanced double displacement equation).

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.9

Formation of barium sulphate and sodium chloride (Page 11).

  • Two Soluble Aqueous Salts: Both reactant solutions (Na2SO4 and BaCl2) are completely clear, colourless, and homogeneous before mixing.
  • Precipitation Phenomenon: When mixed, insoluble barium sulphate instantly nucleates as fine solid particles that form a white precipitate.
  • Definition of Precipitation Reaction: Any chemical reaction in aqueous medium that results in the formation of an insoluble solid (precipitate) is termed a precipitation reaction.

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.9 Formation of barium sulphate and sodium chloride

📌 Key Takeaway: Prototypical double displacement reaction showcasing mutual ion exchange and precipitate formation.

🖼️ Fig. 1.9 – Barium Sulphate Precipitation

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 11

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 1.9 • Barium Sulphate Precipitation

Q1: Write the ionic equation for the precipitation of barium sulphate in Fig. 1.9.

✅ Answer Ba2+(aq) + SO42−(aq) → BaSO4(s)↓

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for correct ionic equation with physical states).

Q2: Why is the reaction in Fig. 1.9 classified as a 'Double Displacement' reaction?

✅ Answer Because there is an exchange of ions between the two reacting compounds: Ba2+ exchanges places with Na+, pairing with SO42− while Na+ pairs with Cl−.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for stating mutual exchange of ions between reactants).

Recall Activity 1.2 Analysis — Lead Nitrate + Potassium Iodide (Page 12)

“Recall Activity 1.2, where you have mixed the solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide:
(i) What was the colour of the precipitate formed? Can you name the compound precipitated?
(ii) Write the balanced chemical equation for this reaction.
(iii) Is this also a double displacement reaction?”

✅ Textbook Solution
(i) Colour and Name of Precipitate:
The precipitate is bright yellow in colour. The compound precipitated is lead(II) iodide (PbI2).
(ii) Balanced Chemical Equation:
Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI2(s)↓ + 2KNO3(aq)
(iii) Classification:
Yes, this is unequivocally a double displacement reaction (as well as a precipitation reaction), because lead ions (Pb2+) and potassium ions (K+) mutually exchange partner anions (I− and NO3−).

📌 Marking Scheme: 3 marks — (1 mark for yellow precipitate of lead iodide + 1 mark for balanced equation + 1 mark for confirming double displacement).

1. MCQ: An iron nail dipped in copper sulphate solution causes the blue solution to turn pale green because:

  2. Iron displaces copper, forming soluble ferrous sulphate
  3. Copper sulphate evaporates leaving water

2. Fill-in-the-Blank: Any aqueous chemical reaction that results in the formation of an insoluble solid is called a _________ reaction.

🔑 Key Words — Sections 1.2.3 & 1.2.4: Displacement & Double Displacement ▼
Displacement Reaction Double Displacement Reaction Precipitation Reaction Precipitate Ferrous Sulphate Barium Sulphate Reactivity Series
  • Displacement Reaction: A reaction in which a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
  • Double Displacement Reaction: A reaction in which two compounds react by exchanging their constituent ions to form two new compounds.
  • Precipitation Reaction: An aqueous double displacement reaction in which an insoluble solid product precipitates out.
  • Precipitate: An insoluble solid compound separated from an aqueous solution during a chemical reaction.
  • Reactivity Series: The relative vertical ranking of metals in decreasing order of their chemical reactivity.
  • Barium Sulphate (BaSO4): Insoluble white heavy precipitate formed by the reaction of barium chloride with sulphate ions.

Activity 1.11 — Oxidation of Copper Powder (Page 12)

  1. Step 1: Take about 1 g of fine reddish-brown copper powder in a porcelain china dish.
  2. Step 2: Place the china dish on a wire gauze mounted over a tripod stand.
  3. Step 3: Heat strongly using a laboratory burner (as shown in Fig. 1.10).
  4. Step 4: Observe the dramatic surface colour transformation.
✅ Observation & Working
1. Formation of Black Coating: The shiny reddish-brown surface of copper powder becomes completely coated with a jet-black substance.
2. Oxidation to Copper(II) Oxide: Oxygen from the air combines chemically with hot copper to form black copper(II) oxide (CuO):
2Cu(s) + O2(g) Heat
→ 2CuO(s) [Black]     (1.28)
3. Reversal by Hydrogen Gas (Reduction): If hydrogen gas is passed over this heated black copper oxide, the black coating turns back into reddish-brown copper metal as oxygen is removed:
CuO(s) + H2(g) Heat
→ Cu(s) [Brown] + H2O(g)     (1.29)

📌 Marking Scheme: 3 marks — (1 mark for black CuO coating + 1 mark for oxidation equation + 1 mark for reversal with H2 gas).

📖 Understanding Fig. 1.10

Oxidation of copper to copper oxide (Page 12).

  • Porcelain China Dish: Heat-resistant ceramic vessel capable of withstanding intense direct flame temperatures without cracking.
  • Wire Gauze & Tripod Stand: Distributes heat evenly across the dish bottom, preventing local hotspots and ensuring uniform oxidation of the copper powder.
  • Black CuO Layer: Copper undergoes an increase in oxidation state (0 → +2) as oxygen atoms insert into the metallic lattice.

Verbatim Caption: Figure 1.10 Oxidation of copper to copper oxide

📌 Key Takeaway: Demonstrates metal oxidation by oxygen addition and its subsequent reversal via chemical reduction with hydrogen.

🖼️ Fig. 1.10 – Oxidation of Copper

📖 Source: Class 10 Science, Page 12

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 1.10 • Oxidation of Copper Powder

Q1: A shiny brown substance 'X' on heating in air becomes black in colour. Identify 'X' and the black substance formed in Fig. 1.10.

✅ Answer Substance 'X' is copper metal (Cu). The black substance formed is copper(II) oxide (CuO).

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for identifying copper + 1 mark for copper(II) oxide / CuO).

Q2: How can the black coating formed in Fig. 1.10 be turned back into the original brown metal? Write the chemical equation.

✅ Answer Pass hot hydrogen gas (H2) over the heated black copper oxide. It reduces the oxide back into brown copper metal:
CuO(s) + H2(g) Heat
→ Cu(s) + H2O(g)

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for passing hydrogen gas over hot CuO + 1 mark for balanced chemical equation).

Oxidation, Reduction & Redox Reactions (Pages 12–13)

🔥 Oxidation
  • Gain of Oxygen: A substance gains oxygen atoms.
  • Loss of Hydrogen: A substance loses hydrogen atoms.
❄️ Reduction
  • Loss of Oxygen: A substance loses oxygen atoms.
  • Gain of Hydrogen: A substance gains hydrogen atoms.
Redox Reaction (Oxidation-Reduction Reaction): A chemical reaction in which one reactant undergoes oxidation while another reactant simultaneously undergoes reduction is called a redox reaction.

Comprehensive Analysis of Reaction (1.30):

CuO + H2 Heat
→ Cu + H2O

  • Reduction of CuO: CuO loses oxygen to become Cu → CuO is reduced to Cu.
  • Oxidation of H2: H2 gains oxygen to become H2O → H2 is oxidised to H2O.
  • Oxidising Agent: CuO (it provides oxygen for oxidation).
  • Reducing Agent: H2 (it removes oxygen from copper oxide).

Other Key Redox Examples in Textbook:

(i) Zinc Oxide + Carbon
ZnO + C → Zn + CO     (1.31)
  • Oxidised: Carbon (C gains oxygen → CO).
  • Reduced: Zinc oxide (ZnO loses oxygen → Zn).
(ii) Manganese Dioxide + Hydrochloric Acid
MnO2 + 4HCl → MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2     (1.32)
  • Oxidised: HCl (loses hydrogen → Cl2).
  • Reduced: MnO2 (loses oxygen → MnCl2).
🔍 Recall Activity 1.1 (Page 13): “In Activity 1.1, magnesium ribbon burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Is magnesium being oxidised or reduced?”
Answer: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. Magnesium metal gains oxygen atoms to form MgO; therefore, magnesium is oxidised.
🌍

1.3 Have You Observed the Effects of Oxidation Reactions in Everyday Life? (Pages 13)

1.3.1 Corrosion

When freshly manufactured, metal articles are shiny and lustrous. However, when left exposed to the atmosphere for some time, their surface gets attacked by environmental chemical agents:

Definition of Corrosion: When a metal is attacked by substances around it such as moisture, oxygen, acids, and atmospheric gases, it is said to corrode, and this destructive process is termed corrosion.
Prominent Examples of Corrosion:
1 Rusting of Iron: Iron articles develop a porous, flaky reddish-brown powder [hydrated ferric oxide, Fe2O3·xH2O] when left exposed to humid air.
2 Black Tarnishing of Silver: Silver ornaments slowly lose their shine and develop a dull black coating of silver sulphide [Ag2S] by reacting with traces of hydrogen sulphide (H2S) in polluted air.
3 Green Patina on Copper: Copper vessels or statues exposed to moist air develop a soft green coating of basic copper carbonate [CuCO3·Cu(OH)2].
⚠️ Economic & Structural Damage: Corrosion causes colossal damage to iron bridges, car bodies, railway tracks, ship hulls, and all metal infrastructure. Every year, billions of rupees are expended worldwide replacing rusted, structurally damaged iron and steel.

1.3.2 Rancidity

💬 Ever Tasted Stale Food?

If you leave edible cooking oil, potato chips, butter, or fried snack packets open to air for weeks, have you noticed that foul smell and rancid, bitter taste? That unpleasant transformation is the result of chemical oxidation!

Definition of Rancidity: When fats and oils present in food materials are oxidised by atmospheric oxygen, they decompose into volatile organic acids and aldehydes, causing them to turn rancid, with an unpleasant change in odour, taste, and nutritional quality.
Methods to Prevent Rancidity:
  • Adding Antioxidants: Substances called antioxidants (such as BHA — Butylated Hydroxyanisole, and BHT — Butylated Hydroxytoluene, or Vitamin E) are deliberately added to commercial oily foods to retard oxidation.
  • Packaging in Inert Gas (Nitrogen Flushing): Potato chip manufacturers flush bags of chips with unreactive nitrogen gas (N2) before sealing, completely displacing atmospheric oxygen to prevent rancidity and breakage.
  • Air-Tight Containers: Storing cooked food in air-tight containers drastically restricts the circulation and availability of fresh oxygen.
  • Refrigeration: Keeping food at low temperatures slows down the kinetic rate of oxidation reactions significantly.
  • Storage Away from Light: Keeping oils and fats away from direct sunlight slows down photochemical oxidation.
❓

NCERT In-Text Questions (Page 13)

Q1. Why does the colour of copper sulphate solution change when an iron nail is dipped in it?
✅ Model Answer
1. Displacement of Copper (Marking Keyword): Iron is more reactive than copper in the reactivity series. When an iron nail is dipped into aqueous blue copper sulphate solution, iron displaces copper ions from the solution.
2. Formation of Ferrous Sulphate: The blue Cu2+ ions are removed from solution and deposited as brown copper metal on the iron nail, while dissolved Fe2+ ions form pale-green ferrous sulphate:
Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) [Blue] → FeSO4(aq) [Pale green] + Cu(s) [Brown deposit]

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for explaining iron is more reactive and displaces copper + 1 mark for balanced equation with colour change blue → pale green).

Q2. Give an example of a double displacement reaction other than the one given in Activity 1.10.
✅ Model Answer
Reaction between Lead Nitrate and Potassium Iodide (Marking Keyword):
When clear colourless aqueous solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide are mixed, a bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide forms instantly alongside soluble potassium nitrate:
Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI2(s)↓ [Yellow precipitate] + 2KNO3(aq)
Alternative Example (Silver Nitrate + Sodium Chloride):
AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s)↓ [White precipitate] + NaNO3(aq)

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for naming reacting pairs + 1 mark for balanced double displacement equation with state symbols).

Q3. Identify the substances that are oxidised and the substances that are reduced in the following reactions.
  1. (i) 4Na(s) + O2(g) → 2Na2O(s)
  2. (ii) CuO(s) + H2(g) → Cu(s) + H2O(l)
✅ Model Answer
(i) 4Na(s) + O2(g) → 2Na2O(s):
  • Substance Oxidised: Sodium (Na) gains oxygen to form Na2O.
  • Substance Reduced: Oxygen (O2) is reduced to oxide ions in Na2O.
(ii) CuO(s) + H2(g) → Cu(s) + H2O(l):
  • Substance Oxidised: Hydrogen (H2) gains oxygen to form H2O.
  • Substance Reduced: Copper(II) oxide (CuO) loses oxygen to form metallic Cu.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for correctly identifying Na oxidised & O2 reduced in part (i); 1 mark for H2 oxidised & CuO reduced in part (ii)).

⚡

Quick Check: Objective Questions (Sections 1.2.5 & 1.3)

1. MCQ: Bags of potato chips are flushed with an inert gas to prevent rancidity. The gas used is:

  1. Oxygen gas
  2. Nitrogen gas
  3. Carbon dioxide gas
  4. Hydrogen gas
✅ Answer (B) Nitrogen gas (N2), because it is chemically inert at ambient temperatures and prevents atmospheric oxidation of oils and fats.

2. True / False: The green coating formed on copper articles upon atmospheric exposure is copper oxide.

✅ Answer False. Copper oxide (CuO) is jet black. The green patina on copper is basic copper carbonate [CuCO3·Cu(OH)2].
🔑 Key Words — Sections 1.2.5 & 1.3: Redox, Corrosion & Rancidity ▼
Oxidation Reduction Redox Reaction Corrosion Rusting Rancidity Antioxidants
  • Oxidation: The chemical process involving the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen (or loss of electrons) by a substance.
  • Reduction: The chemical process involving the loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen (or gain of electrons) by a substance.
  • Redox Reaction: An integrated chemical reaction where oxidation and reduction take place simultaneously.
  • Corrosion: The slow, destructive deterioration of a metal caused by chemical attack of moisture, oxygen, and atmospheric pollutants.
  • Rusting: The specific corrosion of iron in moist air forming brown hydrated ferric oxide (Fe2O3·xH2O).
  • Rancidity: The spoilage and decomposition of fats and oils upon oxidation, producing unpleasant taste and foul odour.
  • Antioxidants: Unreactive chemical compounds added to food products to inhibit or delay oxidation of fats.
📚 6. NCERT Textbook Exercise Solutions & Summary (Pages 14–16)
🧠

What You Have Learnt — Chapter Synthesis (Page 14)

  • Complete Chemical Equation: Represents the reactants, products, and their physical states symbolically.
  • Balancing Imperative: A chemical equation is balanced so that the numbers of atoms of each element are identical on reactant and product sides, strictly satisfying the Law of Conservation of Mass.
  • Combination Reaction: Two or more substances combine chemically to form a single new substance.
  • Decomposition Reaction: A single compound splits into two or more simpler substances upon energy input; exact opposite of combination reactions.
  • Exothermic Reaction: Chemical reactions that release heat energy along with product formation.
  • Endothermic Reaction: Chemical reactions that absorb heat, light, or electrical energy from surroundings.
  • Displacement Reaction: A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from an aqueous solution of its compound.
  • Double Displacement Reaction: Two reacting ionic compounds mutually exchange their ions to form two new compounds.
  • Precipitation Reaction: An aqueous reaction yielding an insoluble solid salt called a precipitate.
  • Redox Processes: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen. Reduction is the loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen.
📝

Complete NCERT Chapter Exercises (Pages 14–16)

1. Which of the statements about the reaction below are incorrect?
2PbO(s) + C(s) → 2Pb(s) + CO2(g)
  1. Lead is getting reduced.
  2. Carbon dioxide is getting oxidised.
  3. Carbon is getting oxidised.
  4. Lead oxide is getting reduced.

Options: (i) (a) and (b)  |  (ii) (a) and (c)  |  (iii) (a), (b) and (c)  |  (iv) all

✅ Model Answer
Correct Choice (Marking Keyword): (i) (a) and (b) are incorrect.
Pointwise Reason:
  • Statement (a) is incorrect because lead oxide (PbO) is reduced to lead, not metallic lead.
  • Statement (b) is incorrect because carbon (C) is oxidised to carbon dioxide, not carbon dioxide.
  • Statements (c) and (d) are chemically correct.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for identifying option (i)).

2. Fe2O3 + 2Al → Al2O3 + 2Fe
The above reaction is an example of a
  1. combination reaction.
  2. double displacement reaction.
  3. decomposition reaction.
  4. displacement reaction.
✅ Model Answer
Correct Option (Marking Keyword): (d) displacement reaction.
Reason: Aluminium (Al) is more reactive than iron (Fe) and displaces iron from ferric oxide (Fe2O3) to form aluminium oxide and molten iron (Thermite process).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for option (d) displacement reaction).

3. What happens when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to iron fillings? Tick the correct answer.
  1. Hydrogen gas and iron chloride are produced.
  2. Chlorine gas and iron hydroxide are produced.
  3. No reaction takes place.
  4. Iron salt and water are produced.
✅ Model Answer
Correct Option (Marking Keyword): (a) Hydrogen gas and iron chloride are produced.
Balanced Equation:
Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) → FeCl2(aq) [Iron(II) chloride] + H2(g)↑ [Hydrogen gas]

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for option (a)).

4. What is a balanced chemical equation? Why should chemical equations be balanced?
✅ Model Answer
1. Definition (Marking Keyword): A chemical equation in which the total number of atoms of each element is equal on both the reactant side (LHS) and product side (RHS) is called a balanced chemical equation.
2. Reason for Balancing (Law of Conservation of Mass): According to the Law of Conservation of Mass, mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The total mass of products must equal the total mass of reactants. This holds true only when the number of atoms of each element remains strictly constant before and after the reaction.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for definition of equal atoms on LHS and RHS + 1 mark for citing the Law of Conservation of Mass).

5. Translate the following statements into chemical equations and then balance them.
  1. (a) Hydrogen gas combines with nitrogen to form ammonia.
  2. (b) Hydrogen sulphide gas burns in air to give water and sulpur dioxide.
  3. (c) Barium chloride reacts with aluminium sulphate to give aluminium chloride and a precipitate of barium sulphate.
  4. (d) Potassium metal reacts with water to give potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
✅ Model Answer
(a) Hydrogen + Nitrogen → Ammonia:
3H2(g) + N2(g) → 2NH3(g)
(b) Hydrogen sulphide + Oxygen → Water + Sulphur dioxide:
2H2S(g) + 3O2(g) → 2H2O(l) + 2SO2(g)
(c) Barium chloride + Aluminium sulphate → Aluminium chloride + Barium sulphate:
3BaCl2(aq) + Al2(SO4)3(aq) → 2AlCl3(aq) + 3BaSO4(s)↓
(d) Potassium + Water → Potassium hydroxide + Hydrogen:
2K(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2KOH(aq) + H2(g)↑ + Heat

📌 Marking Scheme: 4 marks — (1 mark for each correctly translated and balanced equation with correct state symbols).

6. Balance the following chemical equations.
  1. (a) HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 → Ca(NO3)2 + H2O
  2. (b) NaOH + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + H2O
  3. (c) NaCl + AgNO3 → AgCl + NaNO3
  4. (d) BaCl2 + H2SO4 → BaSO4 + HCl
✅ Model Answer
(a) Nitric acid + Calcium hydroxide:
2HNO3(aq) + Ca(OH)2(aq) → Ca(NO3)2(aq) + 2H2O(l)
(b) Sodium hydroxide + Sulphuric acid:
2NaOH(aq) + H2SO4(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l)
(c) Sodium chloride + Silver nitrate:
NaCl(aq) + AgNO3(aq) → AgCl(s)↓ + NaNO3(aq) (Self-balanced)
(d) Barium chloride + Sulphuric acid:
BaCl2(aq) + H2SO4(aq) → BaSO4(s)↓ + 2HCl(aq)

📌 Marking Scheme: 4 marks — (1 mark for each correctly balanced equation).

7. Write the balanced chemical equations for the following reactions.
  1. (a) Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide → Calcium carbonate + Water
  2. (b) Zinc + Silver nitrate → Zinc nitrate + Silver
  3. (c) Aluminium + Copper chloride → Aluminium chloride + Copper
  4. (d) Barium chloride + Potassium sulphate → Barium sulphate + Potassium chloride
✅ Model Answer
(a) Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide:
Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) → CaCO3(s)↓ + H2O(l)
(b) Zinc + Silver nitrate:
Zn(s) + 2AgNO3(aq) → Zn(NO3)2(aq) + 2Ag(s)
(c) Aluminium + Copper chloride:
2Al(s) + 3CuCl2(aq) → 2AlCl3(aq) + 3Cu(s)
(d) Barium chloride + Potassium sulphate:
BaCl2(aq) + K2SO4(aq) → BaSO4(s)↓ + 2KCl(aq)

📌 Marking Scheme: 4 marks — (1 mark for each correctly written balanced chemical equation).

8. Write the balanced chemical equation for the following and identify the type of reaction in each case.
  1. (a) Potassium bromide(aq) + Barium iodide(aq) → Potassium iodide(aq) + Barium bromide(s)
  2. (b) Zinc carbonate(s) → Zinc oxide(s) + Carbon dioxide(g)
  3. (c) Hydrogen(g) + Chlorine(g) → Hydrogen chloride(g)
  4. (d) Magnesium(s) + Hydrochloric acid(aq) → Magnesium chloride(aq) + Hydrogen(g)
✅ Model Answer
(a) Potassium bromide + Barium iodide:
2KBr(aq) + BaI2(aq) → 2KI(aq) + BaBr2(s)
Type: Double Displacement Reaction (and Precipitation).
(b) Zinc carbonate decomposition:
ZnCO3(s) Heat
→ ZnO(s) + CO2(g)
Type: Decomposition Reaction (Thermal Decomposition).
(c) Hydrogen + Chlorine:
H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g)
Type: Combination Reaction.
(d) Magnesium + Hydrochloric acid:
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)↑
Type: Displacement Reaction.

📌 Marking Scheme: 4 marks — (0.5 mark for balanced equation + 0.5 mark for correct reaction type in each subpart).

9. What does one mean by exothermic and endothermic reactions? Give examples.
✅ Model Answer
1. Exothermic Reactions (Marking Keyword): Reactions in which heat energy is released along with the products, increasing the temperature of surroundings.
Example: Burning of natural gas:
CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g) + Heat
2. Endothermic Reactions (Marking Keyword): Reactions in which energy is absorbed from the surroundings (as heat, light, or electricity), causing a temperature drop.
Example: Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate:
CaCO3(s) Heat
→ CaO(s) + CO2(g)

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for exothermic definition + example; 1 mark for endothermic definition + example).

10. Why is respiration considered an exothermic reaction? Explain.
✅ Model Answer
1. Breakdown of Carbohydrates: Food containing carbohydrates (rice, bread, potatoes) is broken down during digestion into simple glucose (C6H12O6).
2. Oxidation in Cells: In cellular respiration, glucose combines with inhaled oxygen inside body cells, breaking down into carbon dioxide and water while liberating a continuous supply of vital energy (ATP) necessary to maintain life:
C6H12O6(aq) + 6O2(aq) → 6CO2(aq) + 6H2O(l) + Energy
3. Conclusion: Because heat/metabolic energy is evolved in the process, respiration is classified as an exothermic reaction.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for explanation of glucose oxidation producing energy + 1 mark for balanced chemical equation).

11. Why are decomposition reactions called the opposite of combination reactions? Write equations for these reactions.
✅ Model Answer
1. Conceptual Contrast (Marking Keyword):
  • In a Combination Reaction, two or more reactant substances unite to form only one single product.
  • In a Decomposition Reaction, a single reactant splits into two or more simpler products upon energy input.
2. Demonstrative Equations:
  • Combination: 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(l)
  • Decomposition: 2H2O(l) Electricity
    →     2H2(g) + O2(g)

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for conceptual distinction: multiple reactants → single product vs single reactant → multiple products + 1 mark for corresponding equations).

12. Write one equation each for decomposition reactions where energy is supplied in the form of heat, light or electricity.
✅ Model Answer
1. Thermal Decomposition (Energy as Heat):
CaCO3(s) Heat
→ CaO(s) + CO2(g)
2. Photochemical Decomposition (Energy as Light):
2AgCl(s) Sunlight
→ 2Ag(s) + Cl2(g)
3. Electrolytic Decomposition (Energy as Electricity):
2H2O(l) Electricity
→ 2H2(g) + O2(g)

📌 Marking Scheme: 3 marks — (1 mark for each correctly balanced equation indicating the specific form of energy over the arrow).

13. What is the difference between displacement and double displacement reactions? Write equations for these reactions.
✅ Model Answer
Feature Displacement Reaction Double Displacement Reaction
Mechanism A more reactive free element displaces a less reactive element from its salt solution. Two reacting compounds mutually exchange their constituent ions to form two new compounds.
Number of Displacements Single displacement occurs. Mutual two-way exchange of ions occurs.
Chemical Equation Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s) Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) → BaSO4(s)↓ + 2NaCl(aq)

📌 Marking Scheme: 3 marks — (1 mark for difference in mechanism + 1 mark for displacement equation + 1 mark for double displacement equation).

14. In the refining of silver, the recovery of silver from silver nitrate solution involved displacement by copper metal. Write down the reaction involved.
✅ Model Answer
1. Chemical Principle: Copper is more reactive than silver in the metal reactivity series, allowing copper to displace silver from silver nitrate solution.
2. Balanced Chemical Equation (Marking Keyword):
Cu(s) + 2AgNO3(aq) → Cu(NO3)2(aq) [Copper(II) nitrate] + 2Ag(s)↓ [Pure silver metal]

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for fully balanced chemical equation with correct formulas and state symbols).

15. What do you mean by a precipitation reaction? Explain by giving examples.
✅ Model Answer
1. Definition (Marking Keyword): Any chemical reaction occurring in aqueous medium that results in the formation of an insoluble solid substance (called a precipitate) that separates out from the solution is termed a precipitation reaction.
2. Example 1 (Barium sulphate):
BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) → BaSO4(s)↓ [White precipitate] + 2NaCl(aq)
3. Example 2 (Lead iodide):
Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI2(s)↓ [Yellow precipitate] + 2KNO3(aq)

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for definition of insoluble precipitate + 1 mark for balanced equation with precipitate flagged).

16. Explain the following in terms of gain or loss of oxygen with two examples each.
  1. (a) Oxidation
  2. (b) Reduction
✅ Model Answer
(a) Oxidation (Gain of Oxygen):
A process in which a substance gains oxygen atoms.
Example 1: Copper powder heated in air gains oxygen: 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO
Example 2: Carbon burning in air gains oxygen: C + O2 → CO2
(b) Reduction (Loss of Oxygen):
A process in which a substance loses oxygen atoms.
Example 1: Copper oxide loses oxygen when heated with hydrogen: CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O
Example 2: Zinc oxide loses oxygen when heated with carbon: ZnO + C → Zn + CO

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for oxidation definition + 2 examples; 1 mark for reduction definition + 2 examples).

17. A shiny brown coloured element ‘X’ on heating in air becomes black in colour. Name the element ‘X’ and the black coloured compound formed.
✅ Model Answer
1. Element 'X' (Marking Keyword): Copper metal [Cu] (characteristic shiny reddish-brown metal).
2. Black Compound Formed (Marking Keyword): Copper(II) oxide [CuO] (formed by oxidation of copper).
3. Chemical Equation:
2Cu(s) [Brown] + O2(g) Heat
→ 2CuO(s) [Black]

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for identifying element X as Copper + 1 mark for identifying black compound as Copper(II) oxide / CuO).

18. Why do we apply paint on iron articles?
✅ Model Answer
1. Physical Barrier Against Air and Moisture (Marking Keyword): Applying paint forms an impermeable, protective barrier over the iron surface.
2. Prevention of Rusting: Rusting of iron requires simultaneous exposure to both atmospheric oxygen and moisture. The coat of paint completely cuts off direct contact between iron and moist air, effectively preventing rust formation.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for stating that paint cuts off air/oxygen and moisture to prevent rusting).

19. Oil and fat containing food items are flushed with nitrogen. Why?
✅ Model Answer
1. Inert Atmosphere (Marking Keyword): Nitrogen (N2) is an unreactive, inert gas that does not react with oils or fats.
2. Prevention of Rancidity: Flushing bags with nitrogen gas expels and replaces atmospheric oxygen. Without oxygen, fats and oils cannot undergo oxidation, thus preserving freshness, taste, and preventing rancidity.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark — (1 mark for explaining that nitrogen creates an inert oxygen-free atmosphere preventing oxidation/rancidity).

20. Explain the following terms with one example each.
  1. (a) Corrosion
  2. (b) Rancidity
✅ Model Answer
(a) Corrosion (Marking Keyword):
The slow chemical deterioration of a metal surface when attacked by moisture, oxygen, acids, and atmospheric pollutants in the surrounding environment.
Example: Rusting of iron — Iron gates and bridges develop a crumbly reddish-brown powder of hydrated ferric oxide [Fe2O3·xH2O] upon exposure to moist air.
(b) Rancidity (Marking Keyword):
The oxidative spoilage and deterioration of food materials containing fats and oils, producing foul odour and unpleasant stale taste.
Example: Butter or potato chips left open to air develop an unpleasant taste and sour rancid smell due to the formation of volatile organic oxidation products.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks — (1 mark for corrosion definition + example; 1 mark for rancidity definition + example).

👥

Group Activity — Exothermic vs Endothermic Explorations (Page 16)

Experimental Protocol:

  1. Take four clean glass beakers and label them A, B, C, and D.
  2. Pour 25 mL of water into beakers A, B, and C; pour 25 mL of blue copper sulphate solution into beaker D.
  3. Measure and record initial temperatures (T1) using a laboratory thermometer.
  4. Add two spatulas of the respective substances:
    • Beaker A: Potassium sulphate (K2SO4)
    • Beaker B: Ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3)
    • Beaker C: Anhydrous copper sulphate (CuSO4)
    • Beaker D: Fine iron filings (Fe)
  5. Stir well and record the final equilibrium temperature (T2).
✅ Experimental Observations & Thermal Classification
Beaker Contents Added Temperature Change (ΔT) Thermal Nature Underlying Chemical Mechanism
A K2SO4 + H2O Negligible change / slight drop (ΔT ≈ −0.5°C) Mildly Endothermic Lattice enthalpy slightly exceeds hydration enthalpy during physical dissolution.
B NH4NO3 + H2O Sharp, noticeable drop (ΔT = −5°C to −8°C) Distinctly Endothermic Large lattice energy absorbed from water molecules to dissociate ammonium and nitrate ions (basis of instant cold packs).
C CuSO4(anhydrous) + H2O Substantial rise (ΔT = +6°C to +10°C) Exothermic Strong hydration energy released as anhydrous white CuSO4 hydrates to form blue pentahydrate [CuSO4·5H2O].
D Fe + CuSO4(aq) Noticeable rise (ΔT = +3°C to +5°C) Exothermic Single displacement reaction: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu + Heat.
Conclusion: Beakers A & B represent Endothermic processes; Beakers C & D represent Exothermic processes.
